newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ's Bolger denies pushing economic doom scenario.
newsitem.headline: NZ's Bolger denies pushing economic doom scenario.

text.p: New Zealand Prime Minister Jim Bolger, embroiled in a controversy over comments by ratings agency Standard and Poor's, denied on Thursday he was using scare tactics over the economic implications of a possible left-wing election victory.
Bolger took issue with comments from an S&P official in New York that a new government was unlikely to depart drastically from current policies.
Bolger said in a radio interview that even a government led by the centre-left Labour Party would need backing from the left-wing Alliance as well as economic nationalist New Zealand First.

"Labour can't form a government by itself. It can't form a government only with New Zealand First. It has to have the active support of the government to do so. The active support of the Alliance would presumably come at a price," Bolger said in a radio interview.
"The Alliance does want to drastically change the policy, they campaign to drastically change the policy. They're quite open about it," he said.

Alliance policies include rewriting the central bank framework to target growth and employment as well as price stability, raising taxes, increasing government spending and imposing higher import tariffs.
The Alliance and NZ First also want to reverse the recent sale of state-owned Forestry Corporation to Fletcher Forest, Brierley Investments and China's Citic.

Bolger, whose conservative government is in danger of losing power in the October 12 poll to a left-wing coalition, has warned interest rates and inflation would rise. Polls suggest the election is finely balanced.
He quoted a newspaper survey saying a quarter of New Zealand chief executives expect investors to pull money out of the country if a left-wing coalition takes power.

"If a quarter of New Zealand CEOs say they're going to take money out of New Zealand if there's a left-wing government after October 12, we should be very nervous. The loss of jobs if we take a quarter of the investment capital away from the major
Bolger denied he was pushing a doom scenario. "I'm not saying this to scare people at all," he said, adding voters were entitled to know the impact of Alliance policies.
